pointers.sentence: Django's design philosophies are a page of its documentation naming the principles it is built by: loose coupling, less code, quick development, don't repeat yourself, explicit over implicit, consistency, and principles of their own for the models, the database API, URLs, templates, views and the cache (`docs/misc/design-philosophies.txt`).
So model, template and view: "MTV" (`docs/faq/general.txt`).
In the code that machinery is the handler, whose centre resolves the path and calls the view (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response`; [Handlers and middleware](../handlers.md)).

The engine, the lexer, the parser and the context import nothing from `django/http/`; the bridge does, `SimpleTemplateResponse`, an `HttpResponse` that renders a template (`django/template/response.py:SimpleTemplateResponse`).

The engine, the lexer, the parser and the context import nothing from `django/http/`; the bridge does, `SimpleTemplateResponse`, an `HttpResponse` that renders a template (`django/template/response.py:SimpleTemplateResponse`).

A request reaches templates all the same, without an import: `RequestContext` holds one and hands it to every context processor, a callable that returns variables for the template from the request (`django/template/context.py:RequestContext`).

`django/db/` imports nothing from the template system, `django/http/` or the views, but its model fields import `django.forms`, so that each can make its own form field (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.formfield`).

The `render` shortcut and `TemplateResponse` ask each engine in `TEMPLATES` in turn, so a view works the same over a Jinja2 backend (`django/template/loader.py:get_template`).

Some of Django's own pages are the exception, among them the debug pages and the fallback when no `"404.html"` is found: each is rendered by an `Engine` (`django/template/engine.py:Engine`) made in the code, in the Django template language whatever `TEMPLATES` names (`django/views/debug.py:DEBUG_ENGINE`).

Some of Django's own pages are the exception, among them the debug pages and the fallback when no `"404.html"` is found: each is rendered by an `Engine` (`django/template/engine.py:Engine`) made in the code, in the Django template language whatever `TEMPLATES` names (`django/views/debug.py:DEBUG_ENGINE`).

A model is a class statement, and `ModelBase.__new__` reads it: it collects the fields, reads the inner `Meta`, and builds the `Options` kept as `Model._meta` (`django/db/models/base.py:ModelBase.__new__`).

A `ModelForm` gets its fields by asking each model field for its form field (`django/forms/models.py:fields_for_model`), and the admin does the same through a hook of its own (`django/contrib/admin/options.py:BaseModelAdmin.formfield_for_dbfield`): a registered model has an editing interface without a line of form code, which is "quick development" at its plainest.

A `ModelForm` gets its fields by asking each model field for its form field (`django/forms/models.py:fields_for_model`), and the admin does the same through a hook of its own (`django/contrib/admin/options.py:BaseModelAdmin.formfield_for_dbfield`): a registered model has an editing interface without a line of form code, which is "quick development" at its plainest.

The schema is written twice, which bends "don't repeat yourself", but the second time by a program: makemigrations compares the models with the state the existing migration files describe and writes the difference as new files (`django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:MigrationAutodetector`), so the second copy is a history of the models' changes.

An instance holds its row's values as attributes and writes itself with `Model.save`; its class holds the human-readable name and the default ordering in `Meta` (`django/db/models/options.py:Options`; [Models and fields](../models.md)).
Nor does a field: whether a field is the primary key, may be null or must be unique is given to it as an argument (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.__init__`).

A model that declares no primary key, and has no parent to take one from, is given a field called `"id"`, of the class `DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD` names unless its application's `AppConfig.default_auto_field` names another (`django/db/models/options.py:Options._prepare`).
One that has no manager, its own or inherited, is given a manager called `"objects"` (`django/db/models/base.py:ModelBase._prepare`).
A field with choices gives its model a method named after the field, get_status_display for a field called status (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.contribute_to_class`).
A foreign key puts on the model at its other end an accessor named after the first model, with "_set" after it (`django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py:ForeignObjectRel.get_accessor_name`).

The documentation calls one mechanism "black magic": to record which templates a view rendered, the test environment replaces `Template._render` with a function that sends `template_rendered` (`django/test/utils.py:setup_test_environment`), a patching that "only happens during test running" (`docs/topics/testing/tools.txt`).

Django 0.95, released in July 2006, merged a branch called magic-removal, "a major refactoring of both the internals and public APIs of Django's object-relational mapper" (`docs/internals/git.txt`).

With 0.95, an application's models stayed in the module that defined them, where before they were "magically transferred" into one namespace of Django's, and a model overrode `save` and `delete` where before it hooked into methods called pre_save and post_save (`docs/releases/0.95.txt`).

Setting an attribute changes only the instance; nothing is written until `Model.save` is called, "rather than the framework saving things behind the scenes silently" (`django/db/models/base.py:Model.save`).
A queryset sends nothing while it is built, runs its query when its results are first needed, and keeps them (`django/db/models/query.py:QuerySet._fetch_all`; [QuerySets](../querysets.md)).

Reading a foreign key whose object is not loaded sends a query for that one object, so a loop that reads it from many instances sends a query for each (`django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py:ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.__get__`).

Another, `FETCH_PEERS`, the "optional performance booster" of "SQL efficiency", fetches the object for every instance the same queryset produced, in one query; an object that `QuerySet.select_related` or `QuerySet.prefetch_related` has loaded needs no fetch (`django/db/models/fetch_modes.py`; [Deferred fields and fetch modes in a queryset](../querysets/deferred.md)).

"Terse, powerful syntax": the double underscores of a keyword argument name a path through relations, as groups__name in a filter of `User` runs through a user's groups to their names, and `Query.setup_joins` turns the path into joins (`django/db/models/sql/query.py:Query.setup_joins`).

The "option to drop into raw SQL easily" is a call away: `QuerySet.raw` maps the rows of an SQL query onto instances (`django/db/models/query.py:QuerySet.raw`), `RawSQL` puts a fragment in an expression, and the connection's cursor runs anything (`django/db/backends/base/base.py:BaseDatabaseWrapper.cursor`).

A URLconf maps a route to a callable, and code that needs a URL asks for it by the pattern's name: `reverse` walks the resolver back from the name to a path (`django/urls/base.py:reverse`; [URL routing](../urls.md)).
`include` mounts an application's patterns under any prefix (`django/urls/conf.py:_path`).

Its answer is the `APPEND_SLASH` setting: when a path without a trailing slash matches no pattern and has produced a 404, and the path with one would resolve to a view not marked `no_append_slash`, `CommonMiddleware` redirects to it (`django/middleware/common.py:CommonMiddleware.should_redirect_with_slash`).

The lexer splits it into text, variables, tags and comments (`django/template/base.py:Lexer.tokenize`; [Templates](../templates.md)); a tag is a name looked up among the registered libraries; a variable is a dotted path, and a callable met on the path is never given arguments: a template can call `BaseManager.all` (`django/template/base.py:Variable._resolve_lookup`).

The database layer sets the flag on its own writes, `Model.save`, `QuerySet.delete`, `QuerySet.update` and the related managers', and the mixin `AltersData` carries it onto a subclass's override (`django/db/models/utils.py:AltersData`).
Reading is allowed: a `{% for %}` over a queryset takes its length, which runs the query (`django/template/defaulttags.py:ForNode.render`).
Inheritance, against redundancy, is `{% extends %}` (`django/template/loader_tags.py:ExtendsNode`).

Custom tags and filters, the "extensibility", are Python registered in a `Library` (`django/template/library.py:Library`). "Be decoupled from HTML" is half kept: the engine renders any text, but its autoescaping, on by default, is HTML's, so a `"<"` in a value comes out as an entity unless the value is marked safe or autoescaping is turned off (`django/template/base.py:render_value_in_context`).

A class-based view enters the URLconf as the function `View.as_view` returns, which makes an instance for each request and calls `View.dispatch` (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.as_view`; [Views](../views.md)).
The request is an argument, not a global, so a test can build one with `RequestFactory` and call a view directly (`django/test/client.py:RequestFactory`).

What Django derives from the request is another matter: the active language, the URLconf and the **script prefix**, the path at which the project is mounted, are kept in state local to the thread or task serving it, set by the handler and the middleware, and read by `gettext` and `reverse` without the request (`django/urls/base.py:set_urlconf`, `django/utils/translation/trans_real.py:activate`).

`GET` is the parsed query string, whatever the method; `POST` is the parsed form body of a "POST" request and empty for any other method (`django/http/request.py:HttpRequest._load_post_and_files`).

`View.dispatch` sends each method in `View.http_method_names` to the view's method of that name in lower case, and `require_http_methods` answers a method not listed with a 405 (`django/views/decorators/http.py:require_http_methods`).
`cache` is a proxy that hands each attribute to the backend of the default alias, so its `get` is the backend's own method, not a wrapper (`django/utils/connection.py:ConnectionProxy`).

Nor does the base class wrap it: `BaseCache.get` only raises `NotImplementedError`, and the local-memory backend's makes the key and reads its store (`django/core/cache/backends/locmem.py:LocMemCache.get`; [Caching, files, mail, signals and tasks](../services.md)).

Consistency is that every backend Django ships is a `BaseCache` (`django/core/cache/backends/base.py:BaseCache`); extensibility, that `"KEY_FUNCTION"` replaces the function that makes a key (`django/core/cache/backends/base.py:get_key_func`).
